page.thesis: The essence of a neural network is not “many nodes,” but the differentiable composition of nonlinear functions. Forward propagation computes the answer, the loss function measures the error, backpropagation uses the chain rule to attribute that error to each parameter, and the optimizer then makes small adjustments accordingly—four steps forming a closed loop that can learn from data.
page.html:
After reading this page, you should be able to answer on your own:
  • Necessity—why linear models cannot handle problems like images and language, while neural networks can.
  • Structure—what the input layer, hidden layer, output layer, nodes, weights, biases, and activation functions are each responsible for.
  • Inference—how an input goes through weighted summation and nonlinear transformation to finally become a prediction.
  • Learning—how loss, gradients, the chain rule, backpropagation, and gradient descent form a closed loop.
  • Math—Understand z = Wx + b, a = φ(z), θ ← θ − η∇L(θ), and be able to hand-calculate one update.
  • Boundaries—when to use it and when not to, and how to recognize overfitting and training failure.
A minimal example used throughout the page　From beginning to end we use only one network as an example:2 inputs → 2 ReLU hidden nodes → 1 Sigmoid output. We use it earlier to explain structure and principles, and in Section 9 we use it to do a complete numerical hand-calculation. You do not need to memorize all notation at once; come back here when needed.

1Why Neural Networks Are NeededIntuition

The core understanding that this section really aims to establish is:Neural networks emerged not because linear models are useless, but because many important relationships in the real world cannot be expressed with a "straight boundary"; through learning nonlinear intermediate features, neural networks enable models to describe these complex relationships.

First, let's look at what a linear model does. Formula

y' = w_1x_1+w_2x_2+…+w_nx_n+b

It indicates that the model multiplies all input features by their respective weights, adds them up, and finally adds a bias term to obtain a prediction score. For example, to predict house prices based on area, age, and distance from city center, you can multiply the three features by their corresponding weights and add them up. The weights indicate the direction and strength of each feature's effect on the result: positive weights generally mean the larger the feature, the higher the prediction score; negative weights mean the larger the feature, the lower the prediction score. Bias b does not depend on any input; it is responsible for adjusting the baseline position of the entire prediction result.

In linear regression, this score can be used directly as the predicted value; in binary classification, the class can be determined by whether the score exceeds a certain threshold. Assuming zero is used as the threshold, the classification boundary is:

w_1x_1+w_2x_2+…+w_nx_n+b=0

When there are only two input features, this boundary is a straight line; with three features it is a plane; in higher dimensions it is called a hyperplane. Although the names differ, the essence is the same: it can only perform a single "flat cut".

This exposes the fundamental limitation of linear models. Suppose there are two classes of points on a plane: one clustered at the center, and the other forming a ring around the center. No matter how you move or rotate a straight line, you cannot completely separate the inner and outer circles, because a correct boundary needs to curve around the center and close. The difficulty here is not that the model has not yet found the "correct straight line", but ratherthe correct answer does not belong to the class of straight-line boundaries at all. Continuing to train a linear model can only search for a relatively better one among many imperfect straight lines, but cannot fundamentally solve the problem.

However, "the original data is not linearly separable" does not mean that linear models can never handle it. You can first manually construct new features. For example, if the difference between the inner and outer circles depends on the distance from a point to the center, then you can compute

r^2=x_1^2+x_2^2

Then have the linear model classify according to r^2 whether it exceeds a certain threshold. In the original x_1,x_2 coordinates, the boundary is a circular curve; but on the new feature r^2 it is just a simple threshold. This illustrates a very important fact:Many so-called nonlinear problems can be transformed into easy-to-handle problems through appropriate feature transformations.

Traditional feature engineering involves humans searching for such transformations. For problems with clear structure and few features, this approach can be very effective. For example, when predicting the motion of an object, you can construct velocity and acceleration; when analyzing financial data, you can construct rate of return, moving average, and volatility. The problem is that when the input is an image, a segment of audio, or a piece of text, the raw dimensionality can reach thousands or even millions, and the truly useful combinations often cannot be enumerated in advance.

Taking image recognition as an example, a single pixel usually has little meaning in itself. To determine whether there is a cat in an image, it may be necessary to first combine adjacent pixels to form edges, then combine edges to form textures and local shapes, then combine local shapes to form ears, eyes, and outlines, and finally synthesize these structures to make a judgment. If entirely relying on humans to manually specify which pixels should be combined and how, not only is the number of combinations huge, but it is also very difficult to cover variations in lighting, angle, pose, and background.

Therefore, the most important value of a neural network is not the superficial "many layers", but rather that during training it canautomatically learn a series of useful feature transformations. After the raw input passes through hidden layers, it is gradually represented as new intermediate features. Taking images as an example, shallow layers may be sensitive to edges and color changes, intermediate layers may combine textures or local structures, and deeper layers may form representations related to complete objects. A specific network may not strictly work according to such human-named levels, but the core idea is: the model no longer requires humans to design all key features in advance; instead, based on the training objective, it finds internal representations from the data that help reduce the error.

Next, we need to understand a point that is prone to misunderstanding: since a single linear transformation has limited capacity, can the problem be solved simply by stacking many linear layers? The answer is no. Suppose the first layer is

h=W_1x+b_1

the second layer is

y=W_2h+b_2

where x is the original input,h is the intermediate result produced by the first layer,y is the final output. Substituting the first layer into the second layer yields:

y =W_2(W_1x+b_1)+b_2; =(W_2W_1)x+(W_2b_1+b_2)

If we let

W=W_2W_1, b=W_2b_1+b_2

then the entire two-layer network becomes:

y=Wx+b

It is still just a single affine transformation. More rigorously speaking here, the biased Wx+b belongs to affine transformations; in everyday explanations it is often loosely called a linear layer. Regardless of the name, the key conclusion remains unchanged:Multiple linear or affine layers without nonlinear activation can be merged into one equivalent layer.

This means that even if such a network has a hundred layers, the types of functions it can express do not essentially change. Although many variables are generated in between, it ultimately can still only form a flat classification boundary. Depth only increases parameter representation and computational process, not the expressive power needed to solve complex nonlinear problems.

What truly changes the situation is adding nonlinear functions between linear transformations. The structure changes from

W_2(W_1x+b_1)+b_2

to something like

W_2 σ(W_1x+b_1)+b_2

where σ is a nonlinear activation function. Since σ cannot be simply merged away like matrix multiplication and addition, so the two layers are no longer equivalent to a single linear layer. The network can repeatedly perform "linear combination—nonlinear transformation—combination again", gradually constructing curved and complex functions and decision boundaries. From this we can see that the power of neural networks comes from the cooperation of two factors: linear layers are responsible for combining information, and nonlinear activation is responsible for breaking the restriction that only flat transformations can be performed.

It is also necessary to avoid misinterpreting "neural networks can express complex relationships" as "any problem should use neural networks". Whether a model is suitable depends on the data and the task. Neural networks are generally suitable for high-dimensional data such as images, text, and speech, as well as problems with complex nonlinear patterns and sufficient training data. But if the data volume is small, the data is mainly structured tables, business rules can be expressed with a few clear rules, or the task requires strict interpretability at every step, then linear models, tree models, or rule systems may be lower cost, faster to train, produce more stable results, and be easier to inspect.

Therefore, this section can be condensed into a complete logical chain:

Linear models can only form flat boundaries → manual feature transformations can solve some nonlinear problems → useful features in high-dimensional complex data are difficult for humans to enumerate exhaustively → neural networks allow the model to learn intermediate features on its own → but simply stacking linear layers is still equivalent to a single layer → nonlinearity must be added for depth to truly gain new expressive power.

2The structure of the network: what it consists ofIntuitionMath

The previous section showed that a neural network cannot gain new expressive power by simply stacking linear transformations; it must insert nonlinearity between linear transformations. This section further answers how these transformations are organized structurally within the network, and what roles the input layer, nodes, hidden layer, and output layer each play.

You can first think of a minimal neural network as an information-processing pipeline:

Input features → hidden layer → output layer → prediction result

For example, a network has two inputs x_1,x_2, one containing two nodes h_1,h_2 hidden layer, and one output node y-hat. Input first goes to both hidden layer nodes simultaneously; the hidden layer each produces a response; these two responses then go to the output node, ultimately producing a prediction. Each connection in the diagram carries a weight that can be adjusted through training, and each non-input node usually also has its own bias.

The input layer is where the network receives data. It usually does not perform real learning computation, but carries the feature vector that has already been converted into numbers x. In tabular tasks, inputs might be age, income, and number of purchases; in image tasks, inputs might be pixel values; in text models, raw words are first converted into numeric vectors before entering the subsequent network. The role of the input layer is not to understand these numbers, but to make explicit for the network which values make up one example.

It is important to note that the meaning and organization of the input numbers are very important. A neural network cannot directly access the real objects themselves; what it sees is always a numerical representation. If the input representation loses key information, no matter how complex the later network is, it cannot recover that information from nothing. For example, if you only give the model the average brightness of an image but ask it to identify the objects in the image, the input itself has not preserved enough shape information.

After the input enters an ordinary node, it first computes:

z=w· x+b=Σ_i w_ix_i+b

Then it computes:

a=φ(z)

These two steps correspond to the two stages inside a node.

The first step is a weighted sum. Each input x_i is multiplied by a weight w_i, all results are summed and then the bias b, giving z. This z is called the pre-activation value, because it is the result before entering the activation function.

The second step is activation. The activation function φ to z transforms it, producing the output that the node actually passes to the next layer a. If the activation function is ReLU, then

a=max(0,z)

Negative pre-activation values become zero, and positive values are preserved. If the output layer uses Sigmoid, then

a=((1) / (1+e^(-z)))

any size of z will be compressed to between 0 and 1, so it is often used to represent a probabilistic output in binary classification.

A node can be understood as a “learnable pattern detector,” but this statement needs to be unpacked. The weight vector w describes the pattern direction the node cares about, the dot product w· x measures how well the current input matches that direction, the bias b adjusts the firing threshold, and the activation function determines how the matching result is converted into a response.

Suppose the input has two features, and a node has weights

w=[2,-1]

bias is -0.5, then it computes:

z=2x_1-x_2-0.5

This means the node tends to respond more when x_1 is large, and x_2 is relatively small. If using ReLU, only when

2x_1-x_2>0.5

will it output a positive number. The bias -0.5 here changes the firing condition: without a bias, the boundary must pass through the origin; with a bias, the boundary can shift as a whole. From this we can see that weights determine the detection direction, and the bias determines the detection threshold.

“One node detects one pattern” is an approximate statement that aids understanding; it does not mean each node necessarily corresponds to a concept that can be clearly named by humans. Some nodes may respond strongly to edges, colors, or word relations, but many nodes learn distributed and abstract mathematical features that are hard to name directly. What really matters is that different nodes can learn different weights and biases, thereby producing different responses to different directions or combinations of the input.

Real tasks usually cannot be completed by relying on a single pattern. Therefore, a hidden layer places multiple nodes to process the same input in parallel. Suppose this layer has m nodes, each node computes its own pre-activation value and activation result:

z_1 =w_1· x+b_1, a_1 =φ(z_1); z_2 =w_2· x+b_2, a_2 =φ(z_2); ⋮ ⋮; z_m =w_m· x+b_m, a_m =φ(z_m)

Arranging their outputs gives a new vector:

a= [a_1; a_2; ⋮; a_m]

Therefore, the output of a layer is usually not a final answer, but a new representation composed of many node responses. Each output component summarizes some aspect of the input, and the next layer treats this new vector as its own input.

This is exactly the core meaning of the hidden layer:The hidden layer does not directly give the task answer, but transforms the raw input into a representation more suitable for subsequent judgment.For example, in an idealized explanation of image recognition, the first layer might respond to horizontal edges, vertical edges, or color changes; the next layer combines these responses into corners or textures; deeper layers continue to combine them into local shapes. The representations learned by real networks are usually more complex than this example, but the logic of transforming representations layer by layer is the same.

“Hidden” does not mean these layers cannot be viewed; rather, training data usually only directly specifies the input and target output, and does not tell the model one by one what each intermediate node should represent. The hidden layer’s representation is formed spontaneously during optimization of the final task. For example, training data only labels images as cat or dog, but does not additionally stipulate that a certain node must detect ears; if ear-related features help reduce classification error, the network may form corresponding responses during training.

When a layer contains many nodes, writing formulas with the same structure one by one becomes tedious. Matrix notation simply combines these calculations. Taking each node’s weight vector as a row of a matrix gives the weight matrix W; arranging each node’s bias into a vector b, the whole layer computation can be written as:

z=Wx+b
a=φ(z)

Suppose the input x has n_(in) components, and this layer has n_(out) nodes, then the shapes of the objects are:

x∈R^(n_(in))
W∈R^(n_(out)× n_(in))

The matrix W's j row is the j node's weights. The matrix multiplication Wx completes all nodes' dot products at once. Therefore, the matrix does not introduce new neural network principles; it is only an efficient way to organize parallel computation.

The output layer is responsible for converting the representation formed by the last hidden layer into the result required by the task. Its specific form depends on the task:

  • A regression task may output only a single unconstrained number, such as predicting temperature or price;
  • A binary classification task usually outputs a number and then converts it through Sigmoid to a result between 0 and 1;
  • A multiclass classification task usually outputs a score for each class and then converts them through Softmax to a class distribution;
  • More complex tasks may output a sequence of words, multiple bounding boxes, or pixel results the same size as the input.

Therefore, the output layer is not a fixed structure; it must match the meaning of the target. Even if the preceding hidden layers are exactly the same, changing the output layer can make the network serve different types of tasks.

Next, consider the number of parameters. For a fully connected layer, every input is connected to every output node. If there are n_(in) inputs and n_(out) nodes, the number of weights is:

n_(in)× n_(out)

Each output node also has one bias, so the number of biases is:

n_(out)

The total number of parameters is:

n_(in)× n_(out)+n_(out)

For a “2 inputs → 2 hidden nodes → 1 output node” network, the first layer has parameters:

2×2+2=6

Among them are 4 weights and 2 biases. The second layer has parameters:

2×1+1=3

Among them are 2 weights and 1 bias. The whole network has a total of:

6+3=9

learnable parameters.

Here “learnable” means these parameters are not hard-coded one by one by the designer, but are continuously adjusted based on error during training. The network structure determines how many layers, how many nodes per layer, and how the nodes connect; training then searches for suitable weights and biases within this predetermined structure. The structure is the container, and the parameters are the specific values that need to be learned in the container.

More parameters usually means the network has greater representational capacity, because it has more degrees of freedom to adjust. But greater capacity does not necessarily mean better performance. Increasing parameters brings at least three costs: more computation is needed, training and inference are slower; more storage and GPU memory are needed; and it is easier to memorize incidental details in the training samples, producing overfitting. On the other hand, a network that is too small may not have enough capacity to express the regularities of the task, forming underfitting.

Therefore, what really needs to be balanced when designing a network is: make the model capacity sufficient to represent the regularities in the task, while also matching the data size, computational resources, and generalization requirements. It is not necessarily true that more nodes or deeper layers are always better.

The structural relationships of this section can be summarized as:

The input layer carries digitized features; weights select and combine information; biases shift the node’s firing threshold; activation functions provide nonlinearity; multiple nodes in parallel form a layer’s new representation; hidden layers gradually make the representation more suitable for the task; the output layer converts the final representation into the required answer; all weights and biases together constitute the parameters to be learned during training.

3Forward Propagation: How the Network Gives AnswersMath

The previous two sections already established two things: a neural network consists of layers of nodes, and each node performs "weighted summation, then passes through an activation function"; nonlinear activation prevents a multi-layer network from collapsing into a linear model. Forward propagation answers the question:when the input and parameters are already given, how does data pass through these layers and ultimately become a prediction result?

"Forward" describes the direction of computation. Starting from the input layer, information flows through each hidden layer in turn and finally reaches the output layer, without going backward in between. Suppose the network has two learnable transformations; its complete computation can be written as:

z^((1))=W^((1))x+b^((1))
a^((1))=φ(z^((1)))
z^((2))=W^((2))a^((1))+b^((2))
y-hat=g(z^((2)))

Here, the superscript (1) and (2) indicate different layers, not squaring.x is the input fed into the network,W^((1)),b^((1)),W^((2)),b^((2)) are the current parameters,φ is the hidden layer activation function,g is the transformation chosen for the output layer according to the task,y-hat is the network's prediction. The hat symbol is used to distinguish "the model's predicted result" from the true target y.

The first step of forward propagation actually occurs before the network computation: converting real-world data into numbers suitable for network processing. Different types of data require different preprocessing. For example, continuous numerical values may need standardization, categories may need encoding, image pixels may need scaling, and text first needs to be converted into tokens and vectors. Preprocessing is not an irrelevant wrapper, because the scale and representation of input values directly affect the information the network subsequently sees.

Taking numerical standardization as an example, suppose one feature ranges from 0 to 1 while another ranges from 0 to 100 units of ten thousand—that is, one million. The latter may naturally contribute much larger values to a weighted sum. Although the network can theoretically compensate by adjusting its weights, doing so often makes training harder. Rescaling features to more reasonable ranges generally makes computation and learning more stable. The same preprocessing rules must be used during both training and actual use; otherwise, even with unchanged network parameters, the meaning of the inputs received by the network will change.

After obtaining the input vector x, the first hidden layer computes:

z^((1))=W^((1))x+b^((1))

This is the weighted sum of all nodes in the layer. The matrix W^((1)) has each row corresponding to the weights of one node, the bias vector b^((1)) provides an independent bias for each node. The resulting z^((1)) is the pre-activation values of all nodes in this layer.

Next, the activation function is applied element-wise to these pre-activation values:

a^((1))=φ(z^((1)))

If the hidden layer uses ReLU, then each component is processed according to the formula max(0,z). Positive values are retained, and negative values become zero. The resulting a^((1)) is no longer just a linear combination of the original input, but a new representation extracted by the first hidden layer according to the current parameters.

This new representation becomes the input to the next layer. That is, the second layer no longer processes the raw features x, but instead processes the a^((1)). If there are more hidden layers, continue repeating:

z^((l))=W^((l))a^((l-1))+b^((l))
a^((l))=φ^((l))(z^((l)))

where l denotes the current layer,a^((l-1)) is the output of the previous layer. The first layer usually treats a^((0)) as the original input x. Therefore, no matter how many layers the network has, forward propagation can be understood as repeatedly performing "linear transformation to produce pre-activation values, then using a nonlinear function to produce a new representation."

We can use the "2-input → 2-hidden-node → 1-output-node" network from the previous section to do a concrete calculation. Suppose the input is:

x=[2; -1]

The hidden layer parameters are:

W^((1))= [1, 1; 2, -1], b^((1))= [0; -1]

First compute the pre-activation values:

z^((1))= [1, 1; 2, -1] [2; -1] + [0; -1] = [1; 4]

If the hidden layer uses ReLU, then:

a^((1))= [max(0,1); max(0,4)] = [1; 4]

Assume the output layer weights and bias are:

W^((2))=[1, -0.5], b^((2))=0

The pre-activation value of the output layer is:

z^((2))=1×1+(-0.5)×4=-1

If this is a binary classification task and the output layer uses Sigmoid, the prediction is:

y-hat=((1) / (1+e^(-(-1))))≈0.269

If we interpret y-hat as the predicted probability of belonging to the positive class, then the network currently thinks the probability of the positive class is about 26.9%. If the classification threshold is set to 0.5, it will predict the negative class. This example shows the entire process of forward propagation: each step is determined by the current input, weights, biases, and activation function, with no random guessing and no modification of parameters during computation.

Which transformation the output layer should use depends on the task requirements. A regression task may directly output z, because the target may be any real number; binary classification tasks often use Sigmoid to compress a score between 0 and 1; mutually exclusive multi-class classification tasks often use Softmax to convert multiple class scores into a distribution that sums to 1. The output transformation must be coordinated with the loss function and the meaning of the target; you cannot use an activation function just because it is common, regardless of the task.

Forward propagation itself is only a computation process and does not mean the network is learning. During actual inference, the network usually performs the following operations: receives a new input, applies the same preprocessing as during training, uses the already determined parameters to complete forward propagation, and then outputs a prediction. Throughout the process, the weights and biases remain unchanged. With the same parameters and the same input, and without additional random mechanisms, the same result will be obtained.

Training includes forward propagation, but does not stop there. During training, first use forward propagation to obtain y-hat, then compare the prediction with the true target y compare, compute the loss. Next, determine how much responsibility each parameter has for the loss and update the parameters in the direction that reduces the loss. Therefore, the logical chain of training is:

input→forward propagation→prediction→compute loss→compute gradient→update parameters

Inference alone typically only includes the first half:

input→forward propagation→prediction

It is important to distinguish the two. Forward propagation answers "what will this network output when the parameters remain at their current values"; the loss function answers "how wrong is this output"; backpropagation answers "which parameters caused these errors and in which direction"; and the optimizer answers "how much should the parameters be changed specifically next". Forward propagation provides the predictions and intermediate calculation results needed for training, but it does not itself correct errors.

This section can be summarized in one sentence:Forward propagation is the process of letting the input pass through "weighted summation and nonlinear transformation" layer by layer according to the network's established structure and current parameters, ultimately forming a prediction that matches the task format; inference ends here, while training still needs to adjust parameters in reverse based on the prediction error.

4Activation Functions: Where Nonlinearity Comes FromIntuitionMath

The previous section left a key question: even if multiple linear or affine layers are stacked very deep, the whole can still be merged into a single affine transformation, so why can neural networks represent curved and complex relationships? The answer is to add activation functions between linear layers.Linear layers are responsible for recombining information, and activation functions are responsible for breaking linearity, enabling these combinations to produce turns, gating, and complex boundaries.

A node usually first computes the pre-activation value:

z=w· x+b

Then the output is obtained through an activation function:

a=φ(z)

If φ(z)=z, the activation function just passes it through unchanged, and the network remains linear. Only when φ is a nonlinear function can the adjacent layers not be simply merged. For example:

y=W_2φ(W_1x+b_1)+b_2

Since φ lies between two linear transformations, it is usually impossible to rearrange the entire expression into a single Wx+b. This seemingly small change is exactly the key to deep networks gaining extra expressive power.

One of the most common hidden layer activations is ReLU:

ReLU(z)=max(0,z)

When z<0, it outputs 0; when z>0, it outputs z. ReLU's graph consists of two straight-line segments, but overall it is not a straight line, because at z=0 it changes slope. This kink is the source of nonlinearity.

A single ReLU node, based on the sign of w· x+b, divides the input space into two regions. In one region the node is off and outputs zero; in the other region the node is active and its output changes linearly with the input. Multiple ReLU nodes with different weights and biases form many boundaries at different positions. Their outputs are then combined by subsequent layers, dividing the input space into more regions.

Therefore, the complex functions formed by ReLU networks can be understood as "piecewise linear": within each small region there is still a linear relationship, but after crossing the activation boundaries of different nodes, the function's slope changes. Just as many short straight-line segments can approximate a circular arc, a large number of nodes and multi-layer combinations can also use many locally flat pieces to piece together an overall curved decision boundary. Here it is not that a single node draws the complete curve alone, but that many nodes jointly provide turns, and subsequent layers combine these turns.

The reasons ReLU is popular include its simple form, cheap computation, and a gradient of 1 on the positive half-axis, so it does not naturally approach zero at large positive or negative inputs like Sigmoid. However, ReLU also has a clear risk: when z<0, the output is constantly zero, and the gradient with respect to z is also zero. If a node stays on the negative half-axis for a long time on training data, it may no longer receive effective updates and keep outputting zero, which is called "dying ReLU".

Leaky ReLU is a direct mitigation method:

LeakyReLU(z)=max(alpha z,z)

where alpha is a small positive number. In this way, the negative half-axis is no longer completely flat but keeps a very gentle slope; the node can still receive gradients in the negative region. However, alpha needs to be set manually or determined in some way, and it can only mitigate some problems; it does not guarantee that all training difficulties will disappear.

The formula for Sigmoid is:

σ(z)=((1) / (1+e^(-z)))

It compresses any real number into the range between 0 and 1.z is very large, the output is close to 1; z is very small, the output is close to 0; z=0the output is 0.5. This range makes it particularly suitable for binary-classification outputs or for gating structures inside a network that need to control how far to open or close.

The problem with Sigmoid is saturation. When the input is in a large positive or negative region, the curve becomes almost flat and the derivative approaches zero. When backpropagation passes through such regions, the gradient may be significantly reduced; if the network has many layers, this reduction accumulates layer by layer, easily causing vanishing gradients. Therefore, although Sigmoid is very common in binary classification output layers, it is usually not the default choice for hidden layers in modern deep networks.

tanh can be written as:

tanh(z)=((e^z-e^(-z)) / (e^z+e^(-z)))

It compresses the input to -1 and 1. Compared with Sigmoid, tanh's output is centered at zero: negative inputs produce negative responses, and positive inputs produce positive responses. This is more convenient in some models. However, both ends of tanh also flatten out, so the problems of saturation and vanishing gradients still exist.

GELU is a common choice in modern Transformer hidden layers. It does not make a hard cutoff at zero like ReLU, but instead performs smooth gating according to the input magnitude: large positive values are mostly retained, large negative values are mostly suppressed, and the transition near zero is smooth. It maintains nonlinearity while being smoother than ReLU, but its computational expression is also more complex. Choosing GELU does not mean that it is necessarily better than ReLU on all tasks; it should be understood more as a commonly used design that has been validated in practice in certain modern architectures.

Softmax does not process a single number, but a set of class scores. For the ith class, it computes:

Softmax(z)_i=((e^(z_i)) / (Σ_j e^(z_j)))

Each output is between 0 and 1, and the sum of all outputs is 1. The larger a class score is relative to the other classes, the higher its output will be. Therefore, Softmax is often used for multi-class classification tasks where classes are mutually exclusive, for example, an image can only be classified as one of "cat, dog, bird".

Softmax outputs are often called class probabilities, but this needs to be understood carefully. It first normalizes the relative scores into a distribution form; whether these values actually match the correct probabilities in reality also depends on the training data, the loss function, and whether the model is well calibrated. A model outputting 0.99 does not automatically guarantee that it has 99% accuracy on all samples where it outputs 0.99.

A point of confusion is that ReLU, Sigmoid, tanh, GELU, and Softmax may all be collectively called activation functions, but their responsibilities in the network are not exactly the same.

The problem faced by hidden layers is: "How to turn the current representation into a new representation that the next layer can continue to combine?" Here the main purpose of using ReLU, GELU, or tanh is to introduce nonlinearity. If all hidden layers have no nonlinearity, no matter how many layers there are, the network will eventually degenerate into a single affine transformation.

The problem faced by the output layer is: "What range and meaning should the final answer have?" Regression tasks may use a linear output, allowing the result to take any real number; binary classification may use Sigmoid to produce a value between 0 and 1; mutually exclusive multi-class classification may use Softmax to produce a class distribution. The transformation in the output layer of course also has mathematical nonlinearity, but the primary reason for choosing it here is to match the task semantics, not to continue constructing hidden representations.

This distinction also explains why the output function cannot be chosen in isolation. The output layer, target encoding, and loss function must be compatible with each other. For example, binary classification often pairs one output score with Sigmoid and binary cross-entropy; mutually exclusive multi-class classification often pairs multiple class scores with Softmax and multi-class cross-entropy; real-valued regression may use a linear output and mean squared error. If the combination does not match, the meaning of the model output, the way the loss is calculated, and the training direction may conflict with each other.

Activation functions are not necessarily better when more complex. Their choice affects representation capacity, gradient propagation, computational cost, and training stability. For ordinary fully connected networks or convolutional networks, ReLU is often a robust starting point for hidden layers; when worried about completely losing gradients in the negative region, Leaky ReLU can be considered; GELU is common in Transformers; Sigmoid and Softmax are more often used according to the output task or gating needs. The final choice should still be based on architecture, data, and actual validation.

This section's logic can be summarized as:Linear layers can only recombine information linearly, and activation functions create turns between these recombinations; many nodes' turns, combined across multiple layers, can piece together complex nonlinear functions. The main task of hidden layer activations is to create composable internal representations, and the main task of the output layer transformation is to convert the final numerical values into answers that match the task's meaning.

5Fundamental Principle: Differentiable Function CompositionIntuition

The previous four sections introduced, respectively, why neural networks need nonlinearity, what components make up a network, how predictions are computed forward, and how activation functions produce nonlinearity. Now we can unify these ideas into one core model:A neural network decomposes a complex mapping into the composition of many simple functions and tries to make these functions differentiable with respect to the parameters, so that it can express complex relationships and also be trained through gradients.

Suppose a network has three layers, and each layer can be viewed as a function:

f_1(x)=φ_1(W_1x+b_1)
f_2(h_1)=φ_2(W_2h_1+b_2)
f_3(h_2)=g(W_3h_2+b_3)

The entire network is:

F(x)=f_3(f_2(f_1(x)))

This relationship of "passing the output of one function to the next" is called function composition. The input x is first converted by f_1 into h_1,h_1 is then converted by f_2 into h_2, and finally by f_3 becomes the prediction. The depth of the network is essentially how many levels of such transformations occur in succession.

Why is function composition valuable? Because complex regularities can often be broken down into several levels of relatively clear simple processing. When recognizing an image, jumping directly from millions of pixels to "this is a cat" in one step is very difficult; if you first form representations of local changes, then combine them into texture and shape evidence, and finally integrate them into a category judgment, the problem is divided into multiple levels of transformation. Neural networks do not necessarily really follow the strict division of labor of "edges–parts–objects" from human language, but function composition allows them to build such hierarchical computation.

Here, every layer is re-encoding information. Re-encoding is not simple copying, nor does it mean the information necessarily becomes richer; rather, it transforms the previous layer's numerical values into a coordinate system that is more convenient for subsequent tasks. For example, the same image is initially represented in pixel coordinates; after passing through several layers, the network may internally form some directions that are more sensitive to shape, texture, or category judgments. Samples that were originally difficult to separate with simple boundaries in pixel space may become easier to separate in the new representation space.

This change can be analogized to choosing a new language for describing the problem. Suppose the task is to distinguish points inside and outside an annulus; in the original coordinates (x_1,x_2) you need a curved boundary; if you re-represent the input as "distance to the center", classification may only require comparing a threshold. What the hidden layers of a neural network do is similar to automatically finding such useful new representations, but it is usually not specified in advance by a human with a concrete formula; instead, training searches for transformations that reduce the final task error.

This is representation learning. Traditional feature engineering has humans decide which features should be extracted; representation learning lets the model automatically adjust intermediate-layer parameters according to the data and objective, forming internal features that help the task. Here it is important to emphasize "helpful for the task": the representations learned by a network are not necessarily good for all uses, nor do they necessarily correspond to concepts that humans easily understand. A network trained for cat-versus-dog classification may retain the information needed to distinguish the classes while ignoring background details irrelevant to classification.

Function composition provides expressive power, but the network must also be trainable. Training needs to answer: if the final prediction is wrong, in which direction should each layer and each parameter be adjusted? This is where "differentiability" comes into play.

If the loss is denoted by L, and the network parameters are denoted by θ, training wants to know:

((∂ L) / (∂ θ))

This derivative describes how the loss changes approximately when the parameter changes by a very small amount. If the derivative is positive, increasing the parameter in the positive direction will locally increase the loss; if the derivative is negative, increasing the parameter will locally decrease the loss. Optimization algorithms use these gradients to find update directions that reduce the loss for a large number of parameters.

Function composition is particularly suitable for this training because the chain rule can pass the final error back layer by layer along the composite relationship. For:

Width (number of nodes per layer)Detect more patterns in parallel at the same level of abstractionParameters, memory usage, and overfitting increase
Depth (number of hidden layers)Express hierarchical structure through more levels of compositionGradient propagation and optimization become harder
F(x)=f_3(f_2(f_1(x)))

The effect of an early parameter on the final loss can be decomposed into its effect on its own layer's output, the effect of that layer's output on the next layer, and so on, until the effect of the final output on the loss. This is exactly the mathematical basis of backpropagation. Forward propagation computes from input to output along the composite function; backpropagation uses the chain rule to compute the gradients of all parameters in reverse, starting from the loss.

Strictly speaking, networks in practice do not require every point to have a derivative that is smooth and continuous in the ordinary sense. ReLU at z=0 is not differentiable, but it is differentiable at other positions, and one can choose an agreed-upon subgradient at the kink, so gradient methods still work. Therefore, "differentiable" here should be understood as: most of the network's computation can provide local change information suitable for backpropagation, rather than requiring every function to be mathematically smooth everywhere.

Network width and depth affect function composition in different ways. Width is the number of nodes in each layer. A wider layer can form more responses in parallel, equivalent to providing more adjustable feature directions at the same stage. But adding nodes usually means more parameters, higher computation and memory requirements, and may also increase the risk of overfitting.

Depth is the number of hidden layers. A deeper network can perform more levels of transformation, combining simple patterns into complex patterns layer by layer. For problems that naturally have hierarchical structure, such composition may be more effective than direct representation in a single layer. But depth also makes optimization harder: gradients must propagate through more layers and may gradually become smaller, become larger, or be disrupted by the scales of different layers. Techniques such as residual connections, normalization, and appropriate initialization largely exist to make deep function composition easier to train.

Both width and depth can increase model capacity, but they cannot simply substitute for each other, nor can model quality be judged solely by the number of parameters. Greater width may allow the same level of representation to contain more patterns, while greater depth allows more sequential levels of combination. What ratio suits a specific task depends on the data structure, computational budget, and training stability.

"Universal approximation" is one of the concepts most easily exaggerated when understanding neural networks. The general idea of the relevant theory is that, under certain conditions, a network with sufficient capacity can approximate many continuous functions to arbitrary precision. It shows that the function family of neural networks has strong expressive power, but it does not guarantee that a training algorithm will necessarily find the required parameters, nor does it say how much data and computation are needed, nor does it guarantee that the model will still be correct on new samples.

Therefore, at least four questions must be kept separate:

First, expressive power: Does the network structure have a set of parameters capable of representing the target relationship?

Second, optimizability: Can existing training methods find good enough parameters within a reasonable time?

Third, sample efficiency: How much representative data is needed to learn this relationship?

Fourth, generalization ability: Does the model remain effective on new samples outside the training data?

A network may theoretically be capable of representing the answer, yet fail to train because of gradient problems; it may also fit the training set very well while merely memorizing samples and failing to generalize; or because the data never contained the key regularity, no matter how large the model is, it cannot learn a reliable relationship. The model can only exploit information present in the training signal; powerful expressive ability cannot conjure facts out of thin air.

What ultimately needs to be remembered from this section is:The "neural" appearance of neural networks is not their most fundamental mathematical feature; a more essential description is a differentiable computational system composed of many small parameterized functions. Function composition allows it to learn representations layer by layer and express complex mappings, while differentiability allows the final error to be passed back to the parameters through the chain rule. Being able to represent, train, learn efficiently, and generalize are four related but not conflatable questions.

6From Internal Values to Answers: Output Layer and LossMath

After the earlier network layers have undergone multiple transformations, the final hidden layer produces a set of internal values. These values are only the representation formed by the model; they are not yet answers to real-world tasks. To make the network trainable, two consecutive translations must be performed:the output layer first translates the internal representation into predictions with task meaning, and the loss function then translates the difference between predictions and true answers into an optimizable scalar.

Suppose the output of the last hidden layer is h, the output layer usually first computes a set of raw scores:

z=W_{ ext{out}}h+b_{ ext{out}}

These raw scores are often called logits. Next, whether to transform z and what transformation to use depends on what the task wants the output to express. The output layer is not a fixed component detached from the task; it is the interface between the model's internal values and real-world answers.

For regression tasks, the target is usually an arbitrary real number, such as housing prices, temperature, or sales. The output layer often uses a linear output, that is, directly setting:

y-hat=z

Here, 'linear' or 'no activation' does not mean the entire network becomes a linear model, because the preceding hidden layers already contain nonlinearity; it only means the final step no longer restricts the output range. If Sigmoid is mistakenly used, predictions will be compressed between 0 and 1, which clearly cannot directly represent typical housing prices. Some regression targets do have range restrictions, in which case a corresponding transformation may also be chosen, but this choice must come from the meaning of the target, not from mechanically applying a template.

For binary classification tasks, usually only one output score is needed z, then pass through Sigmoid:

y-hat=σ(z)=((1) / (1+e^(-z)))

This way y-hat lies between 0 and 1 and can be interpreted as a probability-like score the model assigns to the positive class. For example, y-hat=0.8 indicates that the model strongly favors the positive class, and the score for the negative class is 1-0.8=0.2. If a final class is needed, a threshold must be chosen; 0.5 is a common default, but in tasks where the cost of missed detections and false positives differ, the most suitable threshold may not be 0.5.

For mutually exclusive multi-class classification tasks, the network produces one logit for each class, denoted z_1,…,z_K, then pass through Softmax:

p_k=((e^(z_k)) / (Σ_j e^(z_j)))

All p_k lie between 0 and 1, and their sum is 1. Increasing one class's relative score affects the share of other classes, reflecting competition among classes. This suits tasks where each sample belongs to only one class, such as choosing one of cat, dog, or bird for an image.

Multi-label classification differs from mutually exclusive multi-class classification. An image can simultaneously contain 'person', 'car', and 'night scene'; multiple labels can hold together, so they must not compete for a total share of 1 by passing through Softmax. A common approach is to set up an independent logit for each label and apply Sigmoid separately:

y-hat_k=σ(z_k)

This gives each label its own output between 0 and 1, so increasing the probability of one label does not require decreasing another. The difference between Softmax and multiple Sigmoid outputs is therefore not merely a difference in formulas: they encode two different assumptions about reality—either classes are mutually exclusive or labels can coexist.

After determining the output meaning, we also need to define 'how wrong'. The model cannot directly optimize vague evaluations like 'looks good' or 'basically correct'; it needs a numerical objective. The loss function maps the prediction y-hat and the true answer y into a scalar L. Generally, the smaller the loss, the more the prediction conforms to the training objective.

Let all weights and biases of the network be θ, and write the network prediction as f(x;θ). For a training set containing N samples, the basic objective can be written as:

θ^*=argmin_θ((1) / (N))Σ_(i=1)^(N)L(f(x_i;θ),y_i)

where x_i is the ith input, y_i is its true answer, L is the loss for a single sample; summing and dividing by N gives the average training loss.argmin asks not 'what is the smallest loss?' but 'which set of parameters can make this objective as small as possible.' The training process continuously adjusts θ to try to approach such parameters.

The mean squared error common in regression, for a single scalar prediction, can be written as:

L_(MSE)=(y-hat-y)^2

If the true value is 10 and the prediction is 12, the error is 2 and the squared loss is 4; if the prediction is 20, the error is 10 and the squared loss is 100. Squaring gives larger errors stronger penalties while preventing positive and negative errors from canceling each other out. It also has properties convenient for differentiation. However, MSE is sensitive to abnormally large errors; if the data contains severe outliers, other regression losses may need to be considered.

Binary cross-entropy is common in binary classification:

L_(BCE)=-[ylny-hat+(1-y)ln(1-y-hat)]

When the true label y=1, the second term vanishes and the loss becomes:

L=-lny-hat

The closer the model's probability for the true positive class is to 1, the smaller the loss; if it very confidently gives a probability close to 0, the loss becomes very large. When y=0, the loss becomes -ln(1-y-hat), and the model should give a low probability to the positive class. Cross-entropy cares not only whether the final classification is correct, but also how much probability the model assigns to the correct class.

For example, two models both classify samples above the threshold as positive: model A outputs 0.51, model B outputs 0.99. From an accuracy standpoint, both answer correctly once; but if the true label is positive, cross-entropy considers B's prediction more aligned with the target. Conversely, if the true label is negative, model B's high-confidence error receives a much larger penalty than A. This continuously varying penalty provides detailed signals for gradient training.

If the true label uses one-hot encoding, only the entry corresponding to the true class y_k is 1 and the rest are 0, then the formula simplifies to:

That is, it focuses on checking how much probability the model assigns to the true class. The higher the probability for the true class, the smaller the loss; if the model assigns nearly all probability to the wrong class, the loss is large.

Practical implementations often combine logits and cross-entropy directly in the computation, rather than first explicitly computing Sigmoid or Softmax and then taking the logarithm. This usually has better numerical stability. For example, extremely large or small logits may cause the exponential operation to overflow, or cause probabilities to be rounded to exactly 0, and then computing ln 0 will cause problems. The 'cross-entropy with logits' provided by frameworks usually uses an equivalent but more stable formula. This does not change the output meaning; it only improves the numerical implementation.

Loss functions and evaluation metrics must not be conflated. The loss is the signal for the optimizer to minimize during training, and it usually needs to have usable gradients with respect to model outputs. Evaluation metrics such as accuracy, F1, and AUC are mainly for humans to judge how the model performs against a certain business standard; they are not necessarily suitable for direct differentiation.

Taking accuracy as an example, when the binary classification output changes from 0.49 to 0.48, if the threshold is 0.5, the classification result does not change and accuracy does not change at all; when it changes from 0.49 to 0.51, accuracy suddenly jumps. Such plateaus and jumps cannot provide a smooth direction for every tiny parameter update. Cross-entropy, on the other hand, changes continuously with the predicted probability, so it is more suitable as a training signal.

But a lower optimizable loss does not automatically mean the actual evaluation will be better. The average training loss can decrease while validation set performance worsens, which is a sign of overfitting; the model may also have low cross-entropy but perform poorly on F1 because of an unsuitable threshold. Therefore, during training use loss to guide parameter updates, and during validation and testing use metrics that match the actual goal for evaluation; each has its own role.

The basic objective formula only writes the average loss on the training set. Actual training often adds regularization, class weights, or other constraints, and what is really desired is a model that also works on unseen data, not simply to push training loss to the minimum.θ^* in complex neural networks is usually not a strictly obtainable global optimum, but rather a set of good enough parameters found by the optimization algorithm within limited time.

The complete logic of this section is:The last hidden layer only produces an internal representation; the output layer converts it according to task rules into a real number, a binary classification score, a mutually exclusive class distribution, or multiple independent labels; the loss function then compresses the difference between predictions and true answers into a differentiable scalar; training updates parameters by minimizing this scalar, while metrics such as accuracy, F1, and AUC evaluate the model from the perspective of human task objectives.

7Gradient Descent: Why Move in the Opposite Direction of the GradientMath

The previous section used a loss function to compress prediction error into a scalar, but knowing “how much it is currently wrong” is not enough. A neural network may have thousands or even billions of parameters, and training must further answer:Should each parameter increase or decrease, and by how much, to reduce the loss?The gradient provides the local direction, and the learning rate controls the step size; together they form the basic update of gradient descent.

Let's start with the case of only one parameter θ to understand. The loss is written as L(θ), and its derivative with respect to the parameter is:

((dL) / (dθ))

This derivative describes how the loss changes when the parameter is increased slightly near the current position. If the derivative is positive, increasing θ will cause the loss to rise, so the parameter should be appropriately decreased θ; if the derivative is negative, increasing θ will instead cause the loss to fall, so the parameter should be appropriately increased θ. The two cases can be written uniformly as:

θ←θ-η((dL) / (dθ))

where η>0 is the learning rate. Subtracting the derivative automatically chooses the opposite direction: when the derivative is positive, the parameter decreases; when the derivative is negative, the parameter increases.

When there are many parameters, denote all parameters as the vector θ=[θ_1,θ_2,…,θ_m]^T. The partial derivatives of the loss with respect to each parameter form the gradient:

∇_θ L= [((∂ L) / (∂θ_1)); ((∂ L) / (∂θ_2)); ⋮; ((∂ L) / (∂θ_m))]

The gradient has the same shape as the parameter vector. Each component indicates how the loss responds locally when the corresponding parameter changes slightly. The gradient is not a vague “magnitude of error” but a list of local sensitivities for all parameters.

Why does the gradient indicate the direction of fastest ascent? Suppose that from the current position, moving along the unit direction u by a small step ε, the loss can be expressed by a first-order approximation as:

L(θ+ε u)≈ L(θ)+ε∇ L(θ)· u, \|u\|=1

With the same step size, the change in loss is mainly determined by the dot product ∇ L· u determines. According to the geometric properties of the dot product, when u is in the same direction as the gradient, this value is largest, meaning the loss increases fastest; when u is opposite to the gradient direction, this value is smallest, meaning the loss decreases fastest. Therefore, the locally steepest descent direction is:

-∇ L(θ)

This is the direct reason behind the name “gradient descent”: the gradient itself points in the direction of locally fastest ascent, and taking the negative sign gives the direction of locally fastest descent.

There are two limitations to “fastest” here. First, it compares directions when taking a small step of the same length; if different directions allowed arbitrary step lengths, they could not be compared directly. Second, it relies only on the first-order approximation near the current position, so it is a local conclusion and does not mean the gradient points directly to the global minimum. The loss surface may be curved, narrow, contain saddle points, or have multiple valley floors; the gradient only tells us which side under our feet is steepest and does not provide the entire topographical map.

The original text mentions that there is no unique “slowest descent direction,” which can also be seen from the dot product. If the direction u is perpendicular to the gradient, then:

∇ L· u=0

Under the first-order approximation, the loss is almost unchanged. Choosing a direction nearly perpendicular to the gradient but slightly toward the descent side can make the amount of descent arbitrarily close to zero. Therefore, unlike the clear direction of “steepest descent,” there is no direction with comparable uniqueness for “slowest descent.”

The basic gradient descent update is written as:

θ←θ-η∇_θ L(θ)

The negative gradient determines the direction, and the learning rate η determines the step size. Even if the direction is correct, the step size also determines whether training succeeds. Because the gradient is reliable only in a sufficiently small neighborhood, if a step goes too far, the actual loss surface may already curve elsewhere.

When the learning rate is too small, each step moves only a tiny amount, and the loss may decrease steadily, but training requires many steps with high time and computational cost. In flat regions, updates may even be too small to see almost at all. When the learning rate is too large, the parameter may overshoot the valley bottom and oscillate back and forth between the two sides; in more severe cases, each jump goes to a region with higher loss and larger gradient, eventually causing numerical divergence. A suitable learning rate needs to balance speed and stability, and is often adjusted during training.

Gradient descent does not guarantee finding the global optimum at every step. For deep networks, the loss surface is usually high-dimensional and non-convex, and may contain saddle points, flat regions, and many different low-loss areas. The realistic goal of training is usually not to prove that a unique global minimum has been found, but to find a set of parameters with low training loss and good validation performance within an acceptable computational budget.

Full training begins with parameter initialization. Parameters cannot simply all be initialized to the same value, especially not letting all nodes in the same layer have exactly the same weights; otherwise they will produce the same outputs and the same gradients, and subsequent updates will remain identical, making multiple nodes equivalent to duplicating a single node. Random initialization breaks this symmetry with small differences, giving different nodes the opportunity to learn different patterns. The scale of the random numbers still needs to be reasonable; too large or too small may affect signal and gradient propagation.

A batch of data is then taken for forward propagation. Why is a small batch commonly used instead of looking at only one sample each time, or looking at the entire training set each time? Gradients computed using the full training set are closer to the overall average direction, but the cost of each update is high; single-sample updates are cheap but have large random fluctuations. Mini-batch training provides a compromise among computational efficiency, hardware parallelism, and gradient stability, and is the common way to train modern neural networks.

For the current batch, the network completes forward propagation and obtains predictions, then computes the average loss of the samples in that batch. Backpropagation then uses the chain rule to find the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight and bias. It is necessary to distinguish: backpropagation is responsible for efficiently computing gradients, while gradient descent or another optimizer is responsible for using the gradients to update parameters. The two are closely connected but are not the same step.

The most basic stochastic mini-batch gradient descent updates parameters according to the current gradient; more common optimizers further process the gradient. For example, momentum methods incorporate past update directions to reduce oscillation, and Adam adjusts the effective step size for different parameters based on first-order and second-order statistics of the gradient. No matter how complex the rules are, their common input is still the gradient obtained by backpropagation, and their purpose is still to find parameters with lower loss.

Parameters and hyperparameters must also be distinguished. Parameters are internal values that the model learns during training, such as weights and biases, and they are updated by the optimizer based on gradients. Hyperparameters are set by the trainer or an external search process, such as learning rate, batch size, number of hidden layers, width of each layer, and regularization strength. During training, you cannot just watch the training loss. If the training loss keeps decreasing while the validation loss starts rising, the model may be overfitting to the training data. Training curves can help detect oscillation caused by too large a learning rate, stagnation caused by too small a learning rate, numerical divergence, and overfitting. The final understanding to establish in this section is:The gradient is not a map to the lowest point, but slope information at the current position; for the same small step length, the gradient points to the fastest ascent, and the negative gradient points to the fastest descent. The learning rate determines how far to go along the negative gradient, backpropagation is responsible for computing gradients, the optimizer is responsible for using them, and many repeated updates across batches and epochs together constitute training.

8Backpropagation: How the Chain Rule Distributes ResponsibilityMath

The previous section explained that the optimizer needs the gradient of the loss with respect to each parameter in order to decide the parameter update direction. But a neural network's prediction is produced jointly by many parameters, and the loss function gives only a single final number; it does not directly indicate how much each weight and bias contributed to the result. What backpropagation solves is exactly this computational problem:It uses the chain rule to propagate sensitivity from the loss backward to earlier nodes layer by layer, and to reuse the downstream influences that have already been computed, thereby obtaining the gradients for all parameters in one backward pass.

First, you must distinguish backpropagation from the optimizer. Backpropagation is responsible for computing:

∇_θ L

that is, the gradient of the loss with respect to all parameters. Gradient descent, SGD with momentum, or Adam read these gradients and update parameters according to their own rules. For example, the most basic gradient descent performs:

θ←θ-η∇_θ L

Therefore, backpropagation answers "what is the gradient?", and the optimizer answers "how should parameters be changed after getting the gradient?". Backpropagation itself usually does not modify the weights, so calling it an optimizer is inaccurate.

Let's consider a simplest computation chain. Suppose some weight w affects the loss through the following process:

z=wx+b
a=φ(z)
y-hat=g(a)
L=ell(y-hat,y)

From a causal perspective, w first affects z,z then affects a,a affects the prediction y-hat, and the prediction ultimately affects the loss L. The chain rule writes the entire chain of influences as:

((∂ L) / (∂ w))= ((∂ L) / (∂y-hat))((∂y-hat) / (∂ a))((∂ a) / (∂ z))((∂ z) / (∂ w))

Each term describes only the local influence between two adjacent steps. Multiplying these local derivatives gives the parameter w the total influence on the final loss. This is the mathematical expression of "when a parameter changes slightly, how much does a node change; how much does the node's change cause the next step to change; ultimately how much does the loss change."

We can hand-calculate with a concrete scalar example. Let:

z=wx+b, a=ReLU(z), y-hat=va,

The loss uses:

L=((1) / (2))(y-hat-y)^2

Take x=2,w=1,b=1,v=3,y=5. Forward propagation gives:

z=1×2+1=3
a=ReLU(3)=3
y-hat=3×3=9
L=((1) / (2))(9-5)^2=8

Next, compute backward from the loss. The derivative of the loss with respect to the prediction is:

((∂ L) / (∂y-hat))=y-hat-y=4

The derivative of the prediction with respect to the activation is:

((∂y-hat) / (∂ a))=v=3

Because currently z=3>0, the derivative of ReLU here is:

((∂ a) / (∂ z))=1

The derivative of the pre-activation value with respect to the weight is:

So:

((∂ L) / (∂ w))=4×3×1×2=24

This positive gradient means that near the current point, increasing w will cause the loss to rise, so gradient descent will decrease w. Similarly, we can compute:

((∂ L) / (∂ v))= ((∂ L) / (∂y-hat))((∂y-hat) / (∂ v))=4× a=12

((∂ L) / (∂ b))=4×3×1×1=12

This shows that a single final error can be concretely distributed to multiple parameters through different local derivatives. The "responsibility" here is not responsibility in a moral sense, nor is it splitting the loss into parts and requiring the sum to equal the loss; it represents the local sensitivity of the loss with respect to each parameter.

The sign and magnitude of a gradient must be interpreted relative to the current location. A positive gradient means that increasing the parameter slightly will cause the loss to rise locally; a negative gradient means that increasing the parameter slightly will cause the loss to fall locally. A larger absolute value means the loss is locally more sensitive to changes in this parameter, but it does not necessarily mean that this parameter is globally "more important", nor that it should be modified drastically without limits. The actual update magnitude is also affected by the learning rate, optimizer state, regularization, and other factors.

If you use the most naive method to estimate gradients, you can increase a parameter by a small ε, redo the complete forward propagation, and compare the change in the loss:

((∂ L) / (∂θ_i))≈ ((L(θ_i+ε)-L(θ_i)) / (ε))

This is called finite difference approximation. It is useful for checking whether a small number of gradients are implemented correctly, but it is not suitable for daily training. If a network has one million parameters, perturbing each parameter separately and recomputing the loss would require about one million additional forward computations; the more parameters, the more severe the repeated computation.

The key to backpropagation's efficiency is not the novelty of the chain rule itself, but the reuse of common downstream computations. Suppose many early parameters first affect the same intermediate value a, and then a affects subsequent outputs and losses. The naive method would repeatedly compute for each early parameter "a how it affects the loss after ". Backpropagation computes once first:

((∂ L) / (∂ a))

Then multiply this already obtained downstream sensitivity by the local derivatives of each path entering a to obtain the gradients of earlier variables and parameters respectively. The common later part is computed only once, rather than walking the entire chain again for each parameter.

A network is not always a chain without branches. If a variable affects the loss through multiple paths, its total gradient is the sum of the contributions from all paths. For example, h enters two subsequent branches at the same time, u(h) and v(h), and the loss is L(u,v), then:

((∂ L) / (∂ h))= ((∂ L) / (∂ u))((∂ u) / (∂ h))+ ((∂ L) / (∂ v))((∂ v) / (∂ h))

Influences that occur sequentially along a single path are connected by multiplication, and influences from multiple different paths are summed by addition. These two rules are sufficient to explain how gradients flow in complex networks: multiply along a chain, add across branches.

In practical implementations, forward propagation not only computes predictions but also saves intermediate results needed for backward computation, such as the input to a layer, pre-activation values, or activation values. Backpropagation starts from the loss, processes operations in the reverse order of the forward pass, computes local derivatives for each operation, and passes the gradient received from upstream further to earlier positions. Saving intermediate results consumes memory, which is one reason training usually requires more GPU memory than inference alone.

"Computation graph" is a tool for describing such dependencies: nodes represent values or operations, and edges represent how one result is used by subsequent computations. "Dynamic programming" emphasizes reusing already computed subresults. Understanding these terms helps analyze complex implementations, but the core of backpropagation does not depend on mastering them first. As long as you grasp "compute downstream sensitivity once, then distribute it along all incoming paths", you have understood the fundamental reason for its efficiency.

Backpropagation can also explain the previously mentioned vanishing gradients and exploding gradients. The gradients of early parameters often contain products of local derivatives from many layers. If these factors are less than 1 for a long time, the product may approach zero after repeated multiplication, and early layers receive almost no training signal; if the factors are greater than 1 for a long time, the product may become extremely large, causing instability. This is not backpropagation computing incorrectly, but the chain rule faithfully reflecting how sensitivity changes in deep function composition.

Automatic differentiation frameworks handle much of the differentiation and reuse for us, but they do not change the basic logic. The model first performs forward propagation and records computation relationships, the loss generates an initial gradient, the backward process computes gradients for all parameters according to the chain rule, and finally the optimizer reads the gradients and updates the parameters. Usually, old gradients are cleared or reset before the next batch of data to avoid unintentional accumulation; some training designs deliberately accumulate gradients over multiple batches, but that is an explicit choice.

This section can be summarized as:The loss gives only the final error; backpropagation uses the chain rule to connect "parameter change — intermediate node change — prediction change — loss change". It reuses common downstream influences from the output backward, multiplies derivatives along chains and adds contributions across branches, so one backward pass yields the gradients for all parameters; only after the gradients are computed does gradient descent or Adam update the parameters.

The changes produced by one update are usually small, and it uses only local information provided by one sample or one mini-batch. This section can be summarized as:Forward propagation uses the current parameters to compute predictions and loss; backpropagation starts from the output error and uses the chain rule to obtain the gradient of each layer’s parameters; the optimizer then updates parameters along the negative gradient. Learning is not stuffing the answer into a single node, but rather letting the parameters involved in the current computation across the whole network undergo coordinated fine-tuning, and gradually reducing the overall loss through many repetitions.

10Why Training Can FailEngineering

Understanding forward propagation, loss, backpropagation, and parameter updates does not mean that actual training will certainly succeed. The mathematical formulas describe how training should proceed, but engineering practice must also ensure that the data is correct, numerical values are stable, gradients can propagate, and the model has not merely memorized the training examples.“Training failure” is not a single problem: sometimes parameters cannot learn at all, sometimes values diverge, sometimes the program cuts off gradients, and sometimes the training set performs well but cannot generalize. The first step in diagnosis is to determine which kind of failure it is.

Vanishing gradients occur when the gradients received by earlier layers become extremely small. Backpropagation uses the chain rule, and the gradients of early parameters typically contain the product of many local derivatives across layers. If most of these factors are less than 1, multiplying across many layers can make the result close to zero. At this point, the layers near the output can still update, while the layers near the input barely move, making it difficult for the network to learn effective low-level representations.

Sigmoid and tanh have very small derivatives in their saturation regions, so deep networks that make heavy use of these activations are more prone to vanishing gradients. ReLU or GELU usually improves gradient propagation in a suitable operating range, but they are not a universal solution on their own. Reasonable initialization, normalization, and residual connections control signal scale from different angles or shorten the gradient propagation path, making deep networks easier to train.

Exploding gradients are the opposite phenomenon: when the factors in the chain product or the weight scales are too large, gradients grow rapidly as they propagate toward earlier layers. Parameter updates may suddenly become very large, the loss oscillates violently, and even infinity or NaN appears. Reducing the learning rate can reduce the magnitude of each update; gradient clipping can limit the size when the gradient norm exceeds a threshold; reasonable initialization and normalization try to prevent activation and gradient scales from amplifying layer by layer at the source.
